claim: Cortical neurons remap their receptive fields following sensory nerve damage.
source: Cortical neurons remap their receptive fields and rescale sensitivity to spared peripheral inputs following sensory nerve damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon being investigated in the study.

claim: Cortical neurons rescale sensitivity to spared peripheral inputs following sensory nerve damage.
source: Cortical neurons remap their receptive fields and rescale sensitivity to spared peripheral inputs following sensory nerve damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon being investigated in the study.

claim: Homeostatic adjustments in PV-mediated inhibition during the first days following injury can predict the eventual recovery of cortical sound processing weeks later.
source: Whereas the status of brainstem-evoked potentials did not predict the recovery of sensory responses to surviving nerve fibers, homeostatic adjustments in PV-mediated inhibition during the first days following injury could predict the eventual recovery of cortical sound processing weeks later.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The status of brainstem-evoked potentials did not predict the recovery of sensory responses to surviving nerve fibers.
source: Whereas the status of brainstem-evoked potentials did not predict the recovery of sensory responses to surviving nerve fibers, homeostatic adjustments in PV-mediated inhibition during the first days following injury could predict the eventual recovery of cortical sound processing weeks later.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: Self-regulated inhibitory dynamics are potentially important for the restoration of sensory processing in excitatory neurons following peripheral nerve injuries.
source: These findings underscore the potential importance of self-regulated inhibitory dynamics for the restoration of sensory processing in excitatory neurons following peripheral nerve injuries.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Reorganization following injury involves a rapid unmasking of inputs from adjacent, undamaged regions of the sensory periphery.
source: In sensory cortex, reorganization following injury involves a rapid unmasking of inputs from adjacent, undamaged regions of the sensory periphery and, in cases of incomplete injury, a slower, progressive increase in responsiveness to surviving nerve fibers within the damaged region (Rasmusson, 1982; Merzenich et al., 1983; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992; Kaas et al., 1990; Robertson and Irvine, 1989; Qiu et al., 2000; Chambers et al., 2016; Calford and Tweedale, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In cases of incomplete injury, there is a slower, progressive increase in responsiveness to surviving nerve fibers within the damaged region.
source: In sensory cortex, reorganization following injury involves a rapid unmasking of inputs from adjacent, undamaged regions of the sensory periphery and, in cases of incomplete injury, a slower, progressive increase in responsiveness to surviving nerve fibers within the damaged region (Rasmusson, 1982; Merzenich et al., 1983; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992; Kaas et al., 1990; Robertson and Irvine, 1989; Qiu et al., 2000; Chambers et al., 2016; Calford and Tweedale, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Homeostatic processes may enable the initial stages of reorganization by compensating for dramatic swings in afferent input to maintain neural excitability around a set point.
source: The initial stages of this reorganization may be enabled by homeostatic processes that compensate for dramatic swings in afferent input to maintain neural excitability around a set point (Nahmani and Turrigiano, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Recordings from cortical pyramidal neurons in culture or acute brain slices following sudden shifts in excitatory input have revealed a coordinated sequence of changes at glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses that normalize firing rates and rebalance network activity.
source: Recordings from cortical pyramidal neurons in culture or acute brain slices following sudden shifts in excitatory input have revealed a coordinated sequence of changes at glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses that normalize firing rates and rebalance network activity (Kilman et al., 2002; O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano et al., 1998; Xue et al., 2014; D'amour and Froemke, 2015; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The stabilization of new synaptic inputs from spared regions of the sensory periphery may emerge through a combination of rapid disinhibition and increased structural motility.
source: Whether and how synaptic and extra-synaptic modifications underlie reorganized sensory processing in deafferented zones of the adult cortex remains to be determined, but accumulating evidence from intact preparations suggests that the stabilization of new synaptic inputs from spared regions of the sensory periphery may emerge through a combination of rapid disinhibition and increased structural motility (Li et al., 2014; Marik et al., 2014; Yamahachi et al., 2009; Darian-Smith and Gilbert, 1994; Keck et al., 2011, 2013; Garraghty et al., 1991; Florence et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: A loss of cochlear hair cells and/or cochlear nerve afferent synapses is associated with reduced GABA signaling and cortical hyperexcitability.
source: In the auditory system, a loss of cochlear hair cells and/or cochlear nerve afferent synapses is associated with reduced GABA signaling and cortical hyperexcitability, as manifest in elevated spontaneous firing rates, enhanced central gain and unmasking of sound-evoked responses from undamaged regions of the cochlea (Qiu et al., 2000; Chambers et al., 2016; Seki and Eggermont, 2003; Yang et al., 2012; Scholl and Wehr, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortical hyperexcitability following cochlear damage is manifest in elevated spontaneous firing rates, enhanced central gain and unmasking of sound-evoked responses from undamaged regions of the cochlea.
source: In the auditory system, a loss of cochlear hair cells and/or cochlear nerve afferent synapses is associated with reduced GABA signaling and cortical hyperexcitability, as manifest in elevated spontaneous firing rates, enhanced central gain and unmasking of sound-evoked responses from undamaged regions of the cochlea (Qiu et al., 2000; Chambers et al., 2016; Seki and Eggermont, 2003; Yang et al., 2012; Scholl and Wehr, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons synapse onto pyramidal neuron somata.
source: Nor is it clear whether the decline in GABA markers following peripheral injury arise from a reduced influence of PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons, which synapse onto pyramidal neuron somata and have a well-recognized role in gating activity-dependent cortical plasticity, or instead from other GABA neuron subtypes, which can synapse onto other GABA neurons and exert a net excitatory effect on network activity (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons have a well-recognized role in gating activity-dependent cortical plasticity.
source: Nor is it clear whether the decline in GABA markers following peripheral injury arise from a reduced influence of PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons, which synapse onto pyramidal neuron somata and have a well-recognized role in gating activity-dependent cortical plasticity, or instead from other GABA neuron subtypes, which can synapse onto other GABA neurons and exert a net excitatory effect on network activity (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Some GABA neuron subtypes can synapse onto other GABA neurons and exert a net excitatory effect on network activity.
source: Nor is it clear whether the decline in GABA markers following peripheral injury arise from a reduced influence of PV-expressing fast-spiking interneurons, which synapse onto pyramidal neuron somata and have a well-recognized role in gating activity-dependent cortical plasticity, or instead from other GABA neuron subtypes, which can synapse onto other GABA neurons and exert a net excitatory effect on network activity (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Optetrode assemblies were implanted into the primary auditory cortex (A1) of adult PV-Cre:Ai32 mice.
source: We implanted optetrode assemblies into the primary auditory cortex (A1) of adult PV-Cre:Ai32 mice (Figure 1a) to isolate regular spiking (RS) putative pyramidal neurons based on their spike shape and estimate the strength of local inhibition on RS units during optogenetic activation of PV–expressing GABA neurons (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Regular spiking (RS) putative pyramidal neurons were isolated based on their spike shape.
source: We implanted optetrode assemblies into the primary auditory cortex (A1) of adult PV-Cre:Ai32 mice (Figure 1a) to isolate regular spiking (RS) putative pyramidal neurons based on their spike shape and estimate the strength of local inhibition on RS units during optogenetic activation of PV–expressing GABA neurons (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The strength of local inhibition on RS units was estimated during optogenetic activation of PV-expressing GABA neurons.
source: We implanted optetrode assemblies into the primary auditory cortex (A1) of adult PV-Cre:Ai32 mice (Figure 1a) to isolate regular spiking (RS) putative pyramidal neurons based on their spike shape and estimate the strength of local inhibition on RS units during optogenetic activation of PV–expressing GABA neurons (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The mechanical stability of the optetrode assembly combined with thin, flexible tetrode wires allowed isolation of single units and holding them for many weeks.
source: The mechanical stability of the optetrode assembly combined with the thin, flexible tetrode wires allowed us to isolate single units (Figure 1d) and hold them for many weeks, according to a conservative, objective statistical standard (Figure 1e–f).
evidence: This describes the technical capability of the experimental method.

claim: Auditory responsiveness and local inhibitory tone were measured from individual RS neurons in awake, head-fixed adult mice over a 7-8 week period surrounding varying degrees of auditory nerve injury.
source: With this approach, we could measure auditory responsiveness and local inhibitory tone from individual RS neurons in awake, head-fixed adult mice over a 7–8 week period surrounding varying degrees of auditory nerve injury (Figure 1g).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and measurements made in the study.

claim: PV-expressing FS interneurons could occasionally be isolated on tetrodes but could rarely be held for more than a single recording session.
source: Although we could occasionally isolate PV-expressing FS interneurons on our tetrodes (Figure 1b–c), we could rarely hold these neurons for more than a single recording session (refer to Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: All descriptions of long-term changes in single unit response properties were limited to RS, putative pyramidal neurons.
source: Therefore, all descriptions of long-term changes in single unit response properties were limited to RS, putative pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the analysis based on the experimental observations.

claim: A noise exposure protocol that lesions approximately 50% of high-frequency afferent nerve synapses in the 16-45 kHz region of the cochlea without damaging hair cells was used.
source: We circumvented this problem by selectively eliminating afferent nerve fibers without permanently affecting cochlear mechanics using a well-characterized noise exposure protocol that lesions approximately 50% of high-frequency afferent nerve synapses in the 16–45 kHz region of the cochlea without damaging hair cells (n = 4, Figure 2a) (Wan et al., 2014; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The noise exposure protocol induces only a temporary elevation of the auditory brainstem response (ABR) and distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) thresholds.
source: This protocol induces only a temporary elevation of the auditory brainstem response (ABR) and distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) thresholds, but a permanent reduction in ABR wave 1 amplitude, which has been shown to reflect the permanent elimination of high-frequency cochlear afferent synapses (Figure 2b, the reader is referred to the figure legends and Supplementary file 1 for most statistical reporting) (Liberman and Kujawa, 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data in Figure 2b and citations.

claim: The noise exposure protocol induces a permanent reduction in ABR wave 1 amplitude.
source: This protocol induces only a temporary elevation of the auditory brainstem response (ABR) and distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) thresholds, but a permanent reduction in ABR wave 1 amplitude, which has been shown to reflect the permanent elimination of high-frequency cochlear afferent synapses (Figure 2b, the reader is referred to the figure legends and Supplementary file 1 for most statistical reporting) (Liberman and Kujawa, 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data in Figure 2b and citations.

claim: ABR wave 1 amplitude reflects the permanent elimination of high-frequency cochlear afferent synapses.
source: This protocol induces only a temporary elevation of the auditory brainstem response (ABR) and distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) thresholds, but a permanent reduction in ABR wave 1 amplitude, which has been shown to reflect the permanent elimination of high-frequency cochlear afferent synapses (Figure 2b, the reader is referred to the figure legends and Supplementary file 1 for most statistical reporting) (Liberman and Kujawa, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Several hours after noise exposure, the same unit exhibited elevated response thresholds for a broadband noise burst, slightly reduced PV-mediated inhibition and the appearance of a new, well-tuned low-frequency receptive field that was absent just hours earlier.
source: Several hours after noise exposure that affects high-frequency regions of the cochlea, the same unit exhibited elevated response thresholds for a broadband noise burst, slightly reduced PV-mediated inhibition and the appearance of a new, well-tuned low-frequency receptive field that was absent just hours earlier (Figure 2c–e, second row).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2c-e.

claim: Several hours after noise exposure, firing rates evoked by stimulation of spared, low-frequency cochlear regions had nearly doubled (increased by 96.7%, p=0.04).
source: Several hours after noise exposure, firing rates evoked by stimulation of spared, low-frequency cochlear regions had nearly doubled (increased by 96.7%, p=0.04) with a small, but significant decrease in inhibition (−9.8%, p=0.02) and no significant change in gain or spontaneous rate (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Several hours after noise exposure, there was a small, but significant decrease in inhibition (−9.8%, p=0.02).
source: Several hours after noise exposure, firing rates evoked by stimulation of spared, low-frequency cochlear regions had nearly doubled (increased by 96.7%, p=0.04) with a small, but significant decrease in inhibition (−9.8%, p=0.02) and no significant change in gain or spontaneous rate (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Several hours after noise exposure, there was no significant change in gain or spontaneous rate.
source: Several hours after noise exposure, firing rates evoked by stimulation of spared, low-frequency cochlear regions had nearly doubled (increased by 96.7%, p=0.04) with a small, but significant decrease in inhibition (−9.8%, p=0.02) and no significant change in gain or spontaneous rate (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Six to ten days after noise exposure, inhibition had decreased by 40% (p<0.0001).
source: Six to ten days after noise exposure, inhibition had decreased by 40% (p<0.0001), receptive fields remained focused on spared regions of the cochlea (p<0.01) and spontaneous firing rate was significantly elevated (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: Six to ten days after noise exposure, receptive fields remained focused on spared regions of the cochlea (p<0.01).
source: Six to ten days after noise exposure, inhibition had decreased by 40% (p<0.0001), receptive fields remained focused on spared regions of the cochlea (p<0.01) and spontaneous firing rate was significantly elevated (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: Six to ten days after noise exposure, spontaneous firing rate was significantly elevated (p<0.05).
source: Six to ten days after noise exposure, inhibition had decreased by 40% (p<0.0001), receptive fields remained focused on spared regions of the cochlea (p<0.01) and spontaneous firing rate was significantly elevated (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: Central gain, spontaneous firing rate and frequency tuning all shifted back towards baseline values as response thresholds in the cochlea, ABR and cortical neurons recovered to pre-exposure levels.
source: Central gain, spontaneous firing rate and frequency tuning all shifted back towards baseline values as response thresholds in the cochlea, ABR and cortical neurons recovered to pre-exposure levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the study describing the recovery process.

claim: By approximately 7 weeks after noise exposure, reduced PV-mediated inhibition (−19%, p<0.001) was the only enduring compensatory plasticity marker for the putative loss of high-frequency auditory nerve synapses.
source: By the time of the final recording session, approximately 7 weeks after noise exposure, reduced PV-mediated inhibition (−19%, p<0.001) was the only enduring compensatory plasticity marker for the putative loss of high-frequency auditory nerve synapses.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: In mice, ouabain selectively and evenly eliminates >95% of Type-I spiral ganglion afferent neurons across the frequency map, without affecting other types of sensory and non-sensory cells in the cochlea or auditory nerve.
source: In mice, ouabain selectively and evenly eliminates >95% of Type-I spiral ganglion afferent neurons across the frequency map, without affecting other types of sensory and non-sensory cells in the cochlea or auditory nerve (Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Bilateral ouabain treatment virtually eliminated the ABR without any adverse DPOAE effects in all mice (n = 6).
source: Bilateral ouabain treatment virtually eliminated the ABR without any adverse DPOAE effects in all mice (n = 6, Figure 3b), but, interestingly, was associated with a slow, partial recovery of sound-evoked cortical spiking in half the mice (Figure 3c) but an unremitting loss of auditory responsiveness in the other half (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Bilateral ouabain treatment was associated with a slow, partial recovery of sound-evoked cortical spiking in half the mice.
source: Bilateral ouabain treatment virtually eliminated the ABR without any adverse DPOAE effects in all mice (n = 6, Figure 3b), but, interestingly, was associated with a slow, partial recovery of sound-evoked cortical spiking in half the mice (Figure 3c) but an unremitting loss of auditory responsiveness in the other half (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Bilateral ouabain treatment was associated with an unremitting loss of auditory responsiveness in half the mice.
source: Bilateral ouabain treatment virtually eliminated the ABR without any adverse DPOAE effects in all mice (n = 6, Figure 3b), but, interestingly, was associated with a slow, partial recovery of sound-evoked cortical spiking in half the mice (Figure 3c) but an unremitting loss of auditory responsiveness in the other half (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: When DPOAE thresholds are normal, ABR wave 1b amplitude is an accurate proxy for the number of cochlear afferent synapses.
source: When DPOAE thresholds are normal, ABR wave 1b amplitude is an accurate proxy for the number of cochlear afferent synapses (Wan et al., 2014; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Liberman and Kujawa, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The ABR wave 1b amplitude was not significantly different between mice that recovered auditory processing following ouabain treatment versus those that did not (unpaired t-test, p>0.4).
source: However, the ABR wave 1b amplitude was not significantly different between mice that recovered auditory processing following ouabain treatment versus those that did not (unpaired t-test, p>0.4; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RS units that eventually recovered auditory thresholds exhibited a transient spike in spontaneous firing rate, a sustained increase in central gain and a steep drop in PV-mediated inhibition that began to recover as high-threshold sound-evoked activity returned.
source: RS units that eventually recovered auditory thresholds exhibited a transient spike in spontaneous firing rate, a sustained increase in central gain and a steep drop in PV-mediated inhibition that began to recover as high-threshold sound-evoked activity returned (Figure 3e–h, top row, n = 156).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3e-h.

claim: In RS units that never recovered auditory sensitivity, changes in spontaneous rate were comparatively sluggish, while inhibitory strength declined gradually and monotonically.
source: By contrast, in RS units that never recovered auditory sensitivity, changes in spontaneous rate were comparatively sluggish, while inhibitory strength declined gradually and monotonically (Figure 3e–h, middle row, n = 169).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3e-h.

claim: The dichotomy in the cortical response to nerve injury was shared among all units recorded from a given mouse; if one unit recovered auditory responsiveness, all units recovered auditory responsiveness.
source: This stark dichotomy in the cortical response to nerve injury was shared among all units recorded from a given mouse; if one unit recovered auditory responsiveness, all units recovered auditory responsiveness (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cortical response properties were stable over the recording period in mice with intact auditory nerves (sham surgery control).
source: As a negative control in a separate group of mice (n = 3), we applied sterile water to the round window membrane rather than ouabain and confirmed that cortical response properties were stable over the recording period in mice with intact auditory nerves (Figure 3e–h, bottom row, n = 156).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment supported by data shown in Figure 3e-h.

claim: Spontaneous rate, central gain and inhibition all scaled with the degree of nerve damage.
source: Spontaneous rate, central gain and inhibition all scaled with the degree of nerve damage (Figure 3f–h versus Figure 2g, Figure 4), but varied substantially both over time and between mice.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Restored auditory sensitivity was associated with a sharp loss and partial recovery of inhibition from PV interneurons.
source: Restored auditory sensitivity was associated with a sharp loss and partial recovery of inhibition from PV interneurons, where the degree of eventual recovery could be predicted from changes in inhibition ~1 week after nerve damage (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The degree of eventual recovery could be predicted from changes in inhibition ~1 week after nerve damage.
source: Restored auditory sensitivity was associated with a sharp loss and partial recovery of inhibition from PV interneurons, where the degree of eventual recovery could be predicted from changes in inhibition ~1 week after nerve damage (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: PV-mediated inhibition was a better predictor of sensory recovery than were modifications in spontaneous activity or central gain.
source: Not only was PV-mediated inhibition a predictor of sensory recovery for both mild and severe peripheral damage, but also it was a better predictor than were modifications in spontaneous activity (Figure 4b) or central gain, the biomarkers most commonly employed to assess central auditory plasticity following sensorineural hearing loss (refer to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for an expanded analysis of predictors of recovery).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Just hours after noise exposure, new, low-threshold receptive fields tuned to undamaged regions of the cochlea appeared, accompanied by a small, significant drop in PV-mediated inhibition.
source: Just hours after noise exposure, we observed the appearance of new, low-threshold receptive fields tuned to undamaged regions of the cochlea, accompanied by a small, significant drop in PV-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This is a finding from the study summarized in the Discussion.

claim: Over the ensuing weeks after noise exposure, as cochlear thresholds and cortical receptive field tuning returned to baseline conditions, there was only a brief spike in traditional biomarkers of central auditory hyperactivity, such as increased spontaneous firing rate and increased central gain.
source: Over the ensuing weeks, as cochlear thresholds and cortical receptive field tuning returned to baseline conditions, we noted only a brief spike in traditional biomarkers of central auditory hyperactivity, such as increased spontaneous firing rate and increased central gain.
evidence: This is a finding from the study summarized in the Discussion.

claim: PV-mediated inhibition remained reduced through the final recording session and was the sole physiological indicator for the permanent, presumed loss of high-frequency cochlear synapses.
source: By contrast, PV-mediated inhibition remained reduced through our final recording session and was the sole physiological indicator for the permanent, presumed loss of high-frequency cochlear synapses.
evidence: This is a finding from the study summarized in the Discussion.

claim: The observations are correlative and do not speak to the necessity nor sufficiency of changes in PV networks for functional recovery.
source: Importantly, this is not to say that auditory response normalization was mediated by disinhibition; our observations are correlative and do not speak to the necessity nor sufficiency of changes in PV networks for functional recovery.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from post-synaptic changes in GABA receptors in the RS principal neurons.
source: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from post-synaptic changes in GABA receptors in the RS principal neurons recorded here (Sarro et al., 2008) or from presynaptic changes in the GABA neurons themselves (Marik et al., 2014; Keck et al., 2011; Hengen et al., 2013), as well as many other homeostatic plasticity mechanisms in the RS neurons including upward scaling of glutamatergic synapses (O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano et al., 1998), changes in extrasynaptic GABA or glutamate receptors that mediate tonic currents (Chen et al., 2010; Fleming et al., 2011; Sametsky et al., 2015), or changes in intrinsic membrane response properties (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from presynaptic changes in the GABA neurons themselves.
source: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from post-synaptic changes in GABA receptors in the RS principal neurons recorded here (Sarro et al., 2008) or from presynaptic changes in the GABA neurons themselves (Marik et al., 2014; Keck et al., 2011; Hengen et al., 2013), as well as many other homeostatic plasticity mechanisms in the RS neurons including upward scaling of glutamatergic synapses (O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano et al., 1998), changes in extrasynaptic GABA or glutamate receptors that mediate tonic currents (Chen et al., 2010; Fleming et al., 2011; Sametsky et al., 2015), or changes in intrinsic membrane response properties (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from upward scaling of glutamatergic synapses.
source: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from post-synaptic changes in GABA receptors in the RS principal neurons recorded here (Sarro et al., 2008) or from presynaptic changes in the GABA neurons themselves (Marik et al., 2014; Keck et al., 2011; Hengen et al., 2013), as well as many other homeostatic plasticity mechanisms in the RS neurons including upward scaling of glutamatergic synapses (O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano et al., 1998), changes in extrasynaptic GABA or glutamate receptors that mediate tonic currents (Chen et al., 2010; Fleming et al., 2011; Sametsky et al., 2015), or changes in intrinsic membrane response properties (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from changes in extrasynaptic GABA or glutamate receptors that mediate tonic currents.
source: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from post-synaptic changes in GABA receptors in the RS principal neurons recorded here (Sarro et al., 2008) or from presynaptic changes in the GABA neurons themselves (Marik et al., 2014; Keck et al., 2011; Hengen et al., 2013), as well as many other homeostatic plasticity mechanisms in the RS neurons including upward scaling of glutamatergic synapses (O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano et al., 1998), changes in extrasynaptic GABA or glutamate receptors that mediate tonic currents (Chen et al., 2010; Fleming et al., 2011; Sametsky et al., 2015), or changes in intrinsic membrane response properties (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from changes in intrinsic membrane response properties.
source: Compensation for peripheral damage could have arisen from post-synaptic changes in GABA receptors in the RS principal neurons recorded here (Sarro et al., 2008) or from presynaptic changes in the GABA neurons themselves (Marik et al., 2014; Keck et al., 2011; Hengen et al., 2013), as well as many other homeostatic plasticity mechanisms in the RS neurons including upward scaling of glutamatergic synapses (O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano et al., 1998), changes in extrasynaptic GABA or glutamate receptors that mediate tonic currents (Chen et al., 2010; Fleming et al., 2011; Sametsky et al., 2015), or changes in intrinsic membrane response properties (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fine-scale reorganization varied widely between local subnetworks of RS neurons and the completeness of global remapping was negatively correlated with the spatial extent of peripheral lesions.
source: In classic and contemporary studies of adult cortical plasticity following deafferentation, fine-scale reorganization varied widely between local subnetworks of RS neurons and the completeness of global remapping was negatively correlated with the spatial extent of peripheral lesions (Robertson and Irvine, 1989; Merzenich et al., 1984; Barnes et al., 2015; Keck et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The mode of cortical sensory recovery (complete, partial or none) was roughly shared between all RS units recorded in a given mouse and did not strictly depend on the estimated auditory nerve damage.
source: Here, we report that the mode of cortical sensory recovery (complete, partial or none) was roughly shared between all RS units recorded in a given mouse and did not strictly depend on the estimated auditory nerve damage.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Cochlear ouabain treatment eliminates 95% of primary afferent synapses without affecting sensory transduction mechanisms.
source: Unlike focal ablations of the retina, basilar membrane or skin surface, cochlear ouabain treatment eliminates 95% of primary afferent synapses without affecting sensory transduction mechanisms (Chambers et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The rapid unmasking of excitatory inputs from neighboring undamaged regions of the sensory organ occurs within hours.
source: As compared to the rapid unmasking of excitatory inputs from neighboring undamaged regions of the sensory organ, which occurs within hours (Figure 2, see also [Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992; Calford and Tweedale, 1988]), the recovery of function for spared afferent inputs interspersed within a damaged portion of the nerve, if it occurred at all, unfolded over several weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2 and citations to prior literature.

claim: The recovery of function for spared afferent inputs interspersed within a damaged portion of the nerve, if it occurred at all, unfolded over several weeks.
source: As compared to the rapid unmasking of excitatory inputs from neighboring undamaged regions of the sensory organ, which occurs within hours (Figure 2, see also [Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992; Calford and Tweedale, 1988]), the recovery of function for spared afferent inputs interspersed within a damaged portion of the nerve, if it occurred at all, unfolded over several weeks.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The variable modes of recovery between mice with carefully matched nerve damage may relate to earlier observations that cortical sensory reorganization is not only determined by the pattern and density of peripheral innervation, but may also be directed by activity-dependent differences that are orchestrated through behavioral use.
source: The variable modes of recovery between mice with carefully matched nerve damage may relate to earlier observations that cortical sensory reorganization is not only determined by the pattern and density of peripheral innervation, but may also be directed by activity-dependent differences that are orchestrated through behavioral use (Clark et al., 1988; Xerri et al., 1998; Polley et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Following either type of nerve damage, the cortical networks that recovered function were those that matched the sudden drop in bottom-up excitatory drive with a rapid dip in PV-mediated inhibition.
source: Following either type of nerve damage, the cortical networks that recovered function were those that matched the sudden drop in bottom-up excitatory drive with a rapid dip in PV-mediated inhibition.
